title: Detection of Compromise Infrastructure
summary: This strategy detects compromised infrastructure, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1584 (Compromise Infrastructure). Adversaries often avoid buying anything and instead take over systems that already exist: they hijack a legitimate website and host payloads on it, plant a web shell on a third party server, run command and control through a hacked small business router, or take over an abandoned cloud storage bucket. Detection is almost always indirect, because the compromised equipment belongs to someone else. Useful signals come from external attack surface monitoring, certificate transparency records, passive domain name system data, brand and phishing blocklists, and from your own address space when new services appear on it. The main failure mode is confirmation rather than discovery: a hijacked domain looks legitimate, and by the time a blocklist reports it, the campaign may have moved on. Treat these alerts as takedown and hunting leads, not as proof that your own network is breached.

beginner.definition: Attackers sometimes take over computers or websites that already belong to other people. They do not pay for hosting, and the owner may not know. This detection looks for signs that this hijacked infrastructure is being used against you. It watches for your name, your addresses, and your certificates appearing on systems you do not control.
beginner.whyItMatters: Hijacked infrastructure is hard to block. A site that was safe last month can host malware today, and blocking whole hosting providers breaks real business. Employees trust these pages because they look familiar. If you only check your own network, you will not notice that a partner site or an old domain in your name is now serving phishing pages. Early notice lets you warn users and start a takedown.
howItWorks: You collect outside data: certificates, domain records, blocklists, and internet scans of your own address ranges.
The detection compares new entries with your approved list of assets, suppliers, and brand domains.
It looks for your names or logos appearing on systems that are not registered to you.
It checks whether a known partner or supplier site has started to change quickly or serve new content.
Confirmed matches raise an alert with the asset, the evidence, and the first time it was seen.
The analyst warns users, blocks the specific asset, and starts the takedown process with the provider.
beginner.example: Imagine a chain of shops that suddenly finds its own shop signs appearing on buildings it does not rent. The shops are real, the signs look real, and customers walk in. Nobody broke into the head office; someone reused the brand on a building they took over. The security team only learns about it by walking the streets and looking for its own name.
takeaways: The compromised server usually belongs to someone else, so you detect it from outside, not from your own logs.
Copycat names, strange certificates, and sudden content changes are the signals worth tracking.
Plan the takedown step in advance, because blocking a whole hosting provider hurts your business.

objectives: Describe how adversaries take over existing servers and websites instead of buying new ones
List the external data sources that reveal takeover of infrastructure used against your organisation
Correlate certificate transparency, passive DNS, and brand monitoring findings into one case
Recognise the difference between legitimate supplier changes and a likely hijacked asset
Outline a takedown and user warning workflow that does not require blocking an entire provider
dataSources: Certificate transparency monitoring alerts for certificates that contain your organisation names or lookalike domains
Passive DNS and domain registration monitoring including changes to name servers, mail records, and registration contacts
External attack surface scan results for your own public address ranges showing new listening services
Phishing and malware blocklist feeds that report domains or addresses associated with your brand
Email gateway and web proxy logs showing users visiting or receiving links to suspected copied assets
logic: The detection correlates two kinds of evidence from outside your network: identity, meaning your organisation names, marks, or address ranges appearing on infrastructure registered to someone else, and behaviour, meaning that infrastructure changing quickly, resolving through new name servers, or serving content on paths that mimic your applications. The fields that matter are the domain or address, the certificate subject and issuer, the first-seen and last-changed timestamps, the name server records, and the hosting provider or autonomous system. The benign version is a marketing agency, a franchise partner, or an acquired business running a domain that carries your name with your permission; those assets stay stable, resolve consistently, and are known to a business owner. The malicious version appears without a change ticket, copies login paths, and often reuses your logo with a certificate issued in the last few days.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Brand Appearance or New Service on Infrastructure Not Owned by the Organisation
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   category: threat_intelligence
# detection:
#   selection_brand:
#     query|contains:
#       - example-corp
#       - example-corp-login
#   selection_cert:
#     event.type: certificate_issued
#     certificate.subject|contains: example-corp
#   filter_owned:
#     domain.owner: example-corp
#     destination.asn|in: corporate_asn_list
#   condition: (selection_brand or selection_cert) and not filter_owned
# level: high
falsePositives: Regional franchisees, resellers, and marketing agencies that run approved domains containing the company name
Recently acquired companies whose domains and mail records are still being migrated
Cloud hosting and content delivery providers issuing shared certificates that list many customer names
Security researchers and journalists who register lookalike names to publish warnings about your brand
Legitimate product documentation mirrors and community forums that mention the brand in their own domain names
tuningNotes: Maintain an owned and authorised asset inventory with a named business owner for every entry, and filter those out by ownership record rather than by domain text, because text filters break on lookalikes. Add the certificate issuer to the allowlist only for providers your organisation actually uses, and require an asset to be new or recently changed within the last fourteen days before alerting. Route confirmed matches straight to the abuse contact at the provider, and keep a lower severity feed for the rest as hunting input. The coverage you lose by filtering owned assets is a genuine takeover of your own supplier, so review the supplier list quarterly and monitor their availability and certificate changes separately.
